paper_title: Loud or Silent? A Reusable Framework for Per-Modality Failure Analysis in Multimodal Clinical AI

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal clinical models are usually judged on accuracy with every modality present, but deployment removes modalities; an echocardiogram is often unavailable where an ECG is routine. Two questions then matter beyond the size of the accuracy loss: which modality was responsible, and whether the model fails loudly or silently once that modality is dropped. The distinction is per-example and modality-level, and is separate from post-hoc feature attribution (e.g. SHAP). Models are replaced often; the evaluation that answers these questions is reused. We present a model-agnostic modality-failure framework: given N modality embeddings, any mask-aware probe, and labels, it returns a per-example failure taxonomy, a per-modality complementarity matrix that attributes error to modalities, and a loud-vs-silent dropout profile separating monitorable failures from those that pass unflagged far from the decision boundary, using only deployment-observable signals. We release it as a small, unit-tested harness and validate it against planted ground truth. Across seeds it recovers that planted modality dominance and complementary subset, reports per-modality loud-vs-silent rates, and scales to a three-modality complementarity matrix; because the planted structure is known by construction, this validates recovery of per-example attribution rather than clinical performance. We then instantiate the framework on frozen EchoJEPA and HuBERT-ECG embeddings for LVEF and the EF <= 40% HFrEF gate over a paired MIMIC-IV cohort, where on the held-out test split (n = 245) dropping echo nearly doubles error. The narrow echo-to-ECG overlap that bounds cohort size is itself a deployment finding for cardiac foundation models. All of our work can be found at https://github.com/criticaldata/PRIMED-AI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Foundation models for medical imaging and signals are replaced every few months, while the evaluation that exposes how they fail is reused across model generations. Multimodal clinical models are still judged mostly on accuracy with every modality present. Deployment rarely obliges. model fusing echo and ECG may be trained on both, but at inference the ECG is acquired almost everywhere, while the echo needs equipment and expertise concentrated in well-resourced settings. When modality goes missing, three questions matter that an accuracy number cannot answer. Which modality was responsible for the error? Does the model fail loudly, its output signalling doubt where monitor can catch it, or silently, far from the decision boundary yet wrong and so unflagged? And how do failures distribute across patients? We therefore argue for failure-analysis framework over yet another fusion model, and provide one  (Table 1)  . It is model-agnostic: given modality embeddings, any mask-aware probe, and labels, it returns per-example failure taxonomy, per-modality complementarity matrix, and loud-vs-silent dropout profile, so it transfers across model generations. We instantiate it on frozen EchoJEPA and HuBERT-ECG embeddings (no fine-tuning, realistic stand-in for how small team builds such system) for LVEF regression and the EF 40% HFrEF gate over MIMIC-IV, validate that it recovers planted structure on data with planted ground truth, and demonstrate it on real paired cohort. Scope is deliberately narrow (LVEF / EF 40% only; valvular and HFpEF deferred for label reasons). Contributions. model-agnostic modality-failure framework, with formal definitions for per-example failure taxonomy, per-modality complementarity and attribution, and loud-vs-silent dropout profile that uses only deployment-observable signals. small reusable harness implementing it for any modalities and any mask-aware probe, validated against planted ground truth. Across 12 seeds it recovers the planted dominance and complementary subset, and it scales to an -modality complementarity matrix. An instantiation on frozen echo and ECG embeddings for LVEF/HFrEF over MIMIC-IV, with real-data degradation demonstration on the full paired cohort, together with the observation that the modality expensive to obtain at inference is also the expensive one to build infrastructure for, which we read as deployment finding for cardiac foundation models. Table 1: What the framework reports, and the deployment question each view answers. View Question it answers Failure taxonomy Complementarity matrix Loud-vs-silent profile Are errors merely imprecise, or critical (the clinical gate flips)? Which modality carries the signal, and where are modalities redundant vs. complementary? When modality is missing, does the wrong prediction land near the decision boundary (loud, monitorable) or far from it (silent, unflagged)?

sections.title: 2 Related Work and Positioning
sections.content: Foundation models exist for both modalities: EchoJEPA (Munim et al., 2026) adapts the V-JEPA 2 latentpredictive video approach (Assran et al., 2025) to echocardiography, and HuBERT-ECG (Coppola et al., 2024) is self-supervised model for the 12-lead ECG (HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021) / wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020) family). EchoingECG (Gao et al., 2025) distills echocardiographic knowledge into ECG representations (probabilistic cross-modal embeddings with an echolanguage teacher) so cardiac function can be predicted from the ECG alone, with uncertainty, in zero-/few-shot and fine-tuned settings. Our study differs on three deployment-relevant axes: (i) both backbones stay frozen and we learn only lightweight probes, without distillation or fine-tuning; (ii) we retain and fuse both modalities and ask what happens when one is missing at inference, rather than compressing echo into an ECG-only model; and (iii) inference-time degradation is primary result, and we prespecify demographic fairness audit to apply to full per-example predictions. EchoingECG asks how to build better ECG model using echo at training time; we ask, model-agnostically, 2 how deployed multimodal model fails when modality is gone. Missing-modality robustness is typically reported as single aggregate accuracy drop (Ma et al., 2021, 2022); we instead attribute failures per modality and separate loud from silent degradation, packaged as reusable instrument rather than one-off ablation. This is distinct from post-hoc feature-attribution methods (e.g. SHAP): those explain which input features drove single models prediction, whereas loud-vs-silent operates under actual modality masking and asks where the resulting per-example error lands relative to the clinical decision boundary.

sections.title: 3 A Framework for Modality-Failure Analysis
sections.content: We formalize model-agnostic analysis that assumes only mask-aware predictor: given modalities M, held-out set with regression target (LVEF) and clinical gate = [y τ ] (τ = 40, the HFrEF cut point (Heidenreich et al., 2022)), the HFrEF referral decision (correct when the models gate call matches the patients true EF 40% status, and flipped when it does not), and function (S) returning prediction per example when only the subset is present (others masked at inference), it reports three views. Nothing else about is assumed, so it applies to any probe, fusion architecture, or backbone. (i) Failure taxonomy. Each example, under each condition, is labelled correct (g right, y δ), imprecise (g right, y > δ), or critical (g wrong: an HFrEF case missed or false-alarmed). Critical errors are the clinically actionable failures, and raw mean absolute error (MAE) does not isolate them; large regression error that does not flip the gate stays imprecise by design. (ii) Complementarity and attribution. Each modalitys leave-one-out value is m=MAE(f (M{m})) MAE(f (M)), and per example we attribute the win to the modality whose removal hurts that example most. Solo and pairwise errors form complementarity matrix separating redundant modalities (either alone suffices) from complementary ones (both needed). Views stratify by patient attributes (sex, age, race): modality that wins overall may not win within subgroup, tying attribution to equity. (iii) Loud-vs-silent dropout profile. When is missing, an example that was gate-correct with but is now gate-wrong is an induced critical failure. We split these by deployment-observable signal, the predictions margin from the decision boundary: failure is silent if the wrong prediction sits far on the wrong side (f τ κ, so it looks unremarkable and margin monitor would not flag it) and loud if it lands near the threshold (f τ < κ, where the output invites second read). Margin is proxy for monitorability rather than calibrated confidence (a probabilistic head, cf. EchoingECG, would sharpen it), and it uses only the deployed prediction, never the unavailable full-modality counterfactual. high silent rate is the dangerous regime: wrong, far from the cut, and unflagged. All three views are computed from single call to the released harness.

sections.title: 4 Data and Cohort Design
sections.content: Having defined the modality-failure framework in model-agnostic terms, we now instantiate it in cardiac setting where missing modalities are clinically realistic: frozen echocardiogram and ECG embeddings for LVEF estimation (Lang et al., 2015) and the EF 40% HFrEF gate. We draw on three PhysioNet collections (Goldberger et al., 2000; Pollard et al., 2026): MIMIC-IV-Echo, for DICOM studies from v0.1 (Gow et al., 2023a) and structured LVEF measurements from v1.0 (Gow et al., 2026); MIMIC-IV-ECG, for 12-lead waveforms (Gow et al., 2023b); and MIMIC-IV v3.1 for demographics (Johnson et al., 2024, 2023). Cohort construction runs server-side on BigQuery (MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology, 2024), so the full corpus of roughly 525K DICOM videos across 7,243 studies from 4,579 patients is never materialized locally. LVEF labels. LVEF is not stored in single column, since lab-system transitions and rest/stress protocols yield several structured measurement identifiers (Gow et al., 2026). We prefer direct resting measurement where one exists, falling back to the biplane estimate, then to the explicitly rest-labeled fields, and finally to 3 Table 2: Paired echo and ECG LVEF cohort construction funnel. Step Inclusion criterion Studies Patients 1 2 3 4 5 6 Echo studies (all) Linked to structured measurement Patient has an LVEF reading Patient also has an ECG (subject overlap) ECG within 24 window of the echo Within hospital admission (demographics attached) 7,243 7,182 6,916 6,324 1,678 1,208 4,579 4,552 4,472 4,002 1,326 1, the 3D estimate; ranges are used only when no point estimate is recorded. Stress measurements are excluded, since they describe different physiological state. For auditability we store which field each value came from. From this we derive continuous LVEF and the EF 40% label. Pairing and splits. For each labeled echo study we match the nearest ECG from the same patient within symmetric 24 window, resolving multi-match cases to the nearest timestamp with deterministic tie-breaking. Two alternatives are configurable and matter for how deployment is framed: an asymmetric window, admitting an ECG up to 30 days before the echo but only 24 after, mirrors screen-first setting in which the ECG is the earlier and cheaper test; and encounter-aligned admission pairing is robust to documented ECG clock skew. Splits partition by patient (70/10/20) with an explicit zero-leakage check, and demographics (sex, anchor age, race, and derived age bands) join for the fairness audit, with coverage and MIMIC gender-curation limitations logged. Table 2 reports the construction funnel. Temporal pairing is the binding constraint by wide margin: 6,324 echo studies have subject-level ECG match, but only 1,678 have one within 24 h, and requiring an enclosing hospital admission for demographics leaves 1,208 studies from 1,003 patients. framework about missing modalities therefore meets cohort that is itself defined by how often the two modalities fail to co-occur.

sections.title: 5.1 Frozen encoders and probes
sections.content: This instantiation uses frozen EchoJEPA-L echo-video embeddings (ViT-L, 1024-dim) (Munim et al., 2026), released for MIMIC-IV-Echo on Hugging Face,1 together with frozen HuBERT-ECG embeddings for the 12-lead ECG (Coppola et al., 2024). Both encoders run in inference mode only, and each embedding is tagged with the checkpoint that produced it so results stay traceable to an encoder version. Keeping the backbones frozen is what makes the framework portable: only lightweight probes are trained, so the same evaluation applies unchanged to the next released encoder. Table 3 summarizes the four heads. Echo-only uses attentive pooling (a linear probe on raw highdimensional EchoJEPA tokens is expected to underperform). Cross-attention fusion is the primary model for missing-modality analysis: bidirectional multi-head attention between echo and ECG token sequences, followed by an MLP regression head. All probes predict continuous LVEF; the EF 40% gate is derived from predictions. Metrics: MAE and EF 40% AUROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic) (context only, from cohorts not comparable to our split: EchoJEPA-L reports 5.97 LVEF MAE on an internal Toronto cohort under frozen-backbone multi-view attentive probing (Munim et al., 2026); an AI-ECG screen for EF 35% reports 0.93 AUROC on Mayo cohort (Attia et al., 2019)).

sections.title: 5.2 Evaluation protocol
sections.content: The cross-attention probe is trained once on complete data, and the same deployed checkpoint is then evaluated on the held-out test split under three conditions: full, echo-dropped (an ECG-only deployment), and ECG-dropped (echo-only). Crucially, branch is zeroed at inference rather than retraining unimodal model for each condition. Retraining would answer different question, namely how good model built for one modality can be, whereas the deployment question is what the model you already shipped does when 1https://huggingface.co/datasets/MITCriticalData/mimic-iv-echo-jepa-embeddings 4 Probe Pooling / fusion Role Table 3: Probe architectures and roles. ECG-only mean or attentive Echo-only attentive Concat-MLP concatenated pooled branches into an MLP (each branch pooled as in its unimodal row above) bidirectional cross-attention Cross-attn Ubiquitous-modality baseline; screenfirst lower bound. Upper bound when echo is available; attentive vs. linear ablation. Lightweight fused baseline. Primary fused model; supports branch masking. an input goes missing. We report MAE and EF 40% AUROC per condition, with bootstrap confidence intervals where per-example predictions are available, and plot the degradation curve. This is what separates graceful from silent failure when the expensive modality is absent. The fairness audit is post-hoc on those same test predictions and requires no additional training: we stratify by sex, age band, and race, report per-stratum MAE and EF 40% AUROC, and flag strata falling below minimum count rather than reporting an unreliable number for them. Prespecifying the audit this way keeps it from becoming search over subgroups. Throughout, runs are configuration-driven with fixed random seeds, and each artifact carries manifest recording the git commit and resolved configuration that produced it.

sections.title: 6.1 Validation: the harness recovers planted structure
sections.content: We validate on synthetic echo/ECG data with planted structure, where echo encodes LVEF strongly and ECG weakly, except in an 18% subset where echo is uninformative so ECG must carry the signal. We train one Ridge probe on the full embeddings and mask at inference; splits are stratified by the gate and independent of data generation (test-set HFrEF prevalence held in sane band). This validation is circular by construction: because we plant the modality structure ourselves, checking that the harness recovers it confirms the harnesss mechanics, not that either modality is clinically superior in real patients; this is nonetheless the only place per-example attribution ground truth exists, since no such label is available in real data. Across 12 seeds the harness robustly recovers the planted attribution: echos leave-one-out value is 5.50.7 MAE vs. 1.80.5 for ECG, echo is the more valuable modality in all 12 seeds, and it takes 0.670.04 of per-example wins while ECG correctly wins on the planted complementary subset. The failure taxonomy  (Fig. 1)  shifts from mostly correct under full inference to many critical (gate-flipping) errors when echo is dropped. We also report the loud-vs-silent split per modality; here the two are comparable (0.310.07 silent when echo is dropped vs. 0.320.10 for ECG, with the ordering flipping across seeds). That is the intended behaviour: value and detectability are separate axes the harness measures, not an asymmetry it assumes: the most valuable modality need not be the most dangerous to lose.

sections.title: 6.2 Generality to N modalities
sections.content: With only two modalities, per-example attribution is partly degenerate (dropping one equals using the other), so we exercise the general path on three-modality instance (echo, ECG, and simulated labs channel; n=225 test). The harness returns genuine 33 complementarity matrix  (Fig. 2)  . On the diagonal (each modality alone), echo achieves the lowest MAE 9.7, vs. 12.9 for ECG and 13.4 for labs; off the diagonal, every echo-containing pair (8.3) beats the ECG and labs pair (11.3). The marginal values (echo 3.8, ECG 0.9, labs 0.7) and per-example wins (echo 125, ECG 56, labs 44) recover the planted ordering, flagging echo as irreplaceable and ECG and labs as weak and partly redundant. The same call scales to any . 5 Figure 1: Failure taxonomy by condition (representative seed; gate prevalence held healthy by stratified splitting). Full-modality inference is mostly correct; dropping echo introduces many critical gate-flipping failures. Counts, not just MAE, make the clinically actionable errors explicit. Figure 2: Complementarity matrix on three-modality instance: test MAE with each modality alone (diagonal) and each pair (off-diagonal); lower is better. Every echo-containing combination far outperforms ECG with labs, identifying echo as irreplaceable. Non-trivial attribution of this kind requires 3.

sections.title: 6.3 Real cohort: an integration test
sections.content: Instantiated on real frozen EchoJEPA and HuBERT-ECG embeddings, cross-attention probe on the held-out test split (n=245, the test fold of the full paired cohort) reproduces the expected aggregate dropout  (Table 4)  : dropping echo (the ECG-only deployment) nearly doubles MAE (from 10.28 to 18.57) in this single run. We treat this as an integration test of the end-to-end pipeline rather than validation of the frameworks per-example views, since the taxonomy, complementarity, and loud-vs-silent outputs all require per-example prediction dump on real data. Producing that dump and running the released harness on it is compute-cheap at this cohort size, and canonical rerun with patient-level cross-validation is in progress.

The framework is exposed as small model-agnostic library: single analyze entry point takes modality embeddings, any mask-aware prediction function, and labels, and returns the failure taxonomy, the complementarity matrix, and the loud-vs-silent dropout profile. The same evaluator is therefore reused across probes, fusion architectures, and future backbone releases; Listing 1 shows the call. Listing 1: Using the harness: any modalities, any mask-aware probe. from primed_ai.failure import analyze_modality_failure report = analyze_modality_failure( embeddings={echo: echo_emb, ecg: ecg_emb}, lvef=y, ef_le_40=gate, predict_fn=probe.masked_predict, groups={sex: sex, age_band: age}, # any modalities # regression target + clinical gate # subset -> predictions (others masked) # optional: per-stratum attribution ) report.complementarity[marginal_value] report.dropout[drop_echo][silent_rate] report.conditions[drop_echo][taxonomy] # e.g. {echo: 5.5, ecg: 1.8} # loud vs. silent when echo is missing # correct / imprecise / critical counts What is established, and what remains. The harness recovers planted dominance, complementarity, and silent-failure structure end-to-end, which validates its mechanics but does not substitute for clinical numbers. On the real cohort, first cross-attention run yields the missing-modality degradation of Table 4. What that run does not yet include is the per-example views: the failure taxonomy, complementarity, and loud-vs-silent profile on real predictions, together with the full unimodal-probe sweep, bootstrap confidence intervals, and the fairness stratification. These are matter of exporting per-example predictions and pointing the harness at them, which is compute-cheap at this cohort size, and canonical rerun with patient-level cross-validation in place of the single held-out split is in progress.

sections.title: 8 Modality Asymmetry Beyond Inference Time
sections.content: The asymmetry this framework measures at inference time is not confined to inference time, and noticing that sharpens why the framework is needed. Echocardiography is the harder modality to work with at every stage, not only the harder one to acquire in clinic. No off-the-shelf echo-to-ECG temporal join exists, so windowing, tie-breaking, and leakage-safe splits are all bespoke, and DICOM volume makes echo the heavier 7 modality in development as well. The ECG, cheap and ubiquitous at the bedside, is correspondingly easy on both axes. The two asymmetries therefore point the same way: the modality that is expensive to obtain at inference is also the one whose infrastructure is expensive to build, which is precisely why system is liable to be deployed without it and why knowing how it fails without it matters. We read this correspondence as deployment finding in its own right, and as structural feature of the path from published cardiac foundation model to screening tool rather than an accident of this project.

sections.title: 9 Limitations
sections.content: Several constraints bound our conclusions. MIMIC-IV is single US academic center, so degradation and fairness patterns may not transfer across institutions or acquisition hardware; that is an external-validation gap we cannot close here. By design we never fine-tune the backbones, so absolute accuracy is lower bound on what the representations could achieve, and our claims concern relative degradation under missing modalities rather than state-of-the-art LVEF estimation. We target structured LVEF and the EF 40% gate only, and EF 40% prevalence in paired echo and ECG cohort may be modest, widening AUROC confidence intervals. Two further caveats concern the measures themselves. The loud/silent split uses distance from the EF 40% threshold as proxy for monitorability, not probabilistic confidence; calibrated head would sharpen it. And with =2 the leave-one-out winner equals the surviving-modality solo, so per-example attribution is partly degenerate and is most informative for 3. demographic audit inherits MIMICs known genderand race-curation limitations, small per-stratum samples (giving wide or undefined AUROC), and post-hoc confounding by differing disease prevalence and presentation across groups; observed gaps may reflect the data rather than the model alone. Finally, the current extraction pipeline embeds one DICOM clip per echo study instead of pooling across studys full clip set. This may affect absolute echo-branch accuracy. The fix is known (per-clip caching with pooling at the data-loader level) and is not yet applied to the reported numbers.

sections.title: 10 Discussion
sections.content: The deployment question reframes multimodal value. What matters is less how much fusion adds when both modalities are present than which modality is responsible, and whether the model fails loudly or silently when one is gone. Because the framework assumes only mask-aware predictor, it transfers to the next echo or ECG backbone without change; the evaluation outlives the model it was built to evaluate, which is why we release an instrument rather than checkpoint. Our validation study shows why the two axes have to be measured rather than assumed: echo-dominance was robust across seeds, yet the loud-vs-silent rates of the two modalities were comparable, so value and detectability need not coincide. Design philosophies for epistemic virtue in clinical AI, such as BODHI (Cajas Ordonez et al., 2026), therefore need this kind of measurement: calibrated humility presupposes knowing which failures are visible in the first place. Future work extends the instrument along that same line: further modalities, calibrated per-example profiles, and the same measurement repeated across datasets and hospital settings, where failure profile that shifts between institutions is what tells deployed system when to defer rather than answer. Designing for humility needs measurement of that kind, not assertion of it.
